sentences.text: The name Styracosaurus translates to "spiked lizard," a title derived from Ancient Greek words for a spike and a lizard.
Styracosaurus albertensis measured approximately 5.5 to 5.8 meters in length and stood about 1.65 meters high at the hips.
This dinosaur possessed large nasal horns and frills that were among the most distinctive facial features of all dinosaurs.
The nasal horn of Styracosaurus could reach 60 centimeters in length and 15 centimeters in width.
Evidence suggests the frill of the holotype specimen broke during the animal's life and was shortened by approximately 6 centimeters.
A 2015 skull discovery suggests that individual variation in Styracosaurus horn asymmetry was likely commonplace.
The discovery of 100 individuals at an Arizona site indicates that Styracosaurus lived in herds like other ceratopsians.

Paleontologists Gregory S. Paul and Per Christiansen proposed that large ceratopsians like Styracosaurus could walk faster than an elephant, based on possible tracks showing no signs of forelimb extension.
The genus was named by Lawrence Lambe in 1913.
The first fossil was discovered in the summer of 1913 by Charles H. Sternberg during a Geological Survey of Canada expedition along the Red Deer River.
Darren Tanke of the Royal Tyrrell Museum relocated the lost site of S. parksi in the summer of 2006.
Styracosaurus were herbivores that likely fed mostly on low-growing vegetation due to the position of their heads.
Its skull featured a beak and shearing cheek teeth in continuous dental batteries, indicating a diet of sliced plants.
Styracosaurus may have been capable of knocking down taller plants using their horns, beak, and large body size.
Researchers long believed Styracosaurus used its frills and horns for defense against large predatory dinosaurs.
The large frill of Styracosaurus may have helped regulate body temperature by increasing surface area, similar to elephant ears.

Researchers suggest the mass death of Styracosaurus at the Dinosaur Park Formation site may have occurred when non-herding animals gathered around a waterhole during a drought in a seasonal, semi-arid environment.
Styracosaurus is classified as a member of the subfamily Centrosaurinae.
S. sphenocerus was originally described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1890 as a species of Monoclonius and later attributed to Styracosaurus in 1915.
McDonald and Horner reclassified S. ovatus into the new genus Rubeosaurus based on phylogenetic analysis.
The species S. parksi is now generally accepted as a specimen of S. albertensis.
This extinct herbivorous dinosaur lived during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous in North America.
Fossils of Styracosaurus have been found in the Dinosaur Park Formation near Steveville, Alberta.
Evidence suggests that the lineage leading to Styracosaurus originated in Asia during the Jurassic, with true horned ceratopsians appearing in North America by the early Late Cretaceous.
The classification of S. ovatus is debated, having been moved to Rubeosaurus in 2010 but considered again as a species of Styracosaurus or even S. albertensis since 2020.
A 2020 study by Robert Holmes and colleagues found that the type specimen of Rubeosaurus ovatus falls within the morphological variation of S. albertensis.
